speechtext:
Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 201, to amend the Penitentiaries Act. He said:
The principal clauses of the Bill and the principal purpose sought to be attained by it are to make provision to enable the carrying on, on a larger scale, of industrial work in penitentiaries. There are other provisions of a less important nature, and I might, perhaps, just mention them before I take up the most important ones. There are quite a number of provisions repealing sections of the existing Act because, in view of legislation in regard to classification under the Civil Service Act, they serve practically no purpose. There is a provision extending the definition of a penitentiary so as to make it include a hospital in which a convict may be detained. There is provision made for enabling the minister to constitute an advisory board composed of officials to advise with him concerning the administration of penitentiaries. There is a provision making more clear the definition of the duties of a warden. There is a provision dealing with fines that may be imposed by the warden, and with his power of suspension. There is a disposition with regard to uniforms to be supplied to officers and purchases which it is permissible fo rthem to make of articles manufactured in the penitentiaries. Then there are other provisions which are dealt with because,
IMr. Meighen-J
as a matter of fact, by the effect of subsequent legislation and the practice of carrying on penitentiaries, they have become practically obsolete. They were provisions which looked to treating each penitentiary as a separate orgarrization by itself under the executive control of the warden, giving him control of purchases and so forth. The effect of subsequent legislation has been that these sections have fallen into disuse, and they are simply repealed.
There is a provision with regard to visitors, making more clear the present provision. I do not think it substantially modifies the present provision. There is a provision to enact that when a man is sentenced to a penitentiary, he shall be sentenced to such penitentiary as the minister shall from time to time designate. Under the present section, the court is required to sentence him to the penitentiary of the province, but there is power in the minister to transfer him to any other penitentiary. As we have recently done away with one of the penitentiaries, a provision assuming that there is a penitentiary in each province becomes inapplicable, and, in fact, it was not strictly applicable even in the past. There is a provision requiring that the judge or judicial officer who pronounces sentence shall prepare a schedule giving information and details elicited from the convict himself as to his past and so forth. This, it is considered, will be useful information to those taking charge of the convict. There is a provision enabling the minister, who now has to sign every order for transfer from one penitentiary to another, to authorize an officer to do that instead. There are provisions, which, I think, may be described as making more clear and more effective the present provisions with regard to the manner of dealing with insane convicts. I do not think there is any substantial modification. Likewise, there is a provision as to dealing with convicts suffering from infectious or contagious diseases, which provision also makes more clear existing legislation. There is a provision dealing with the detention of female convicts, making it possible, which will seem to be very desirable, if it be found practicable, to provide an absolutely separate institution for them. There are provisions making more clear the existing disposition as regards the remission of part time of sentences for good conduct on the part of the convicts. There is also a provision requiring that the convicts shall be furnished with a copy of

the regulations so that they may know what laws they are living under.
Then we come to the provisions to which I have referred. In substance, it is enacted that the different departments of Government shall, where that is practically possible, procure from the penitentiaries such things as they require and which can be produced in the penitentiary. There are dispositions following on that, providing for the details as to how the penitentiaries shall be compensated for the goods so furnished. It is not intended that there shall be an actual payment of money from one department to the other, but there are ^different provisions establishing a method of determining what sum of money as a whole should be allotted to the penitentiaries administration as compensation for the work so done. Then there are provisions for the allotment as between the convicts out of this money of what may be found available in the way of remuneration for their labour, after taking into consideration the cost of maintenance of the penitentiaries, and so forth.
There is a provision making more severe the penalties to which officers are subjected for the offence of trafficking with convicts, and regulating the question of the burden of proof when an officer is charged with being in possession of or dealing with articles with which he is forbidden to deal under the law or the regulations of the penitentiary.
There is a section providing for and adding to what is required presently to be given to a convict upon his discharge from the penitentiary, principally in the way of clothing, and to some extent in the way of an allowance of money. That covers the dispositions of the Bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. JACQUES BUREAU (Three Rivers and St. Maurice) :
speechtext:
With the consent of
the House I would like to ask a question, and make a suggestion to the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty). The question I desire to ask is whether the Bill now presented to the House is based on the reports made by the Commissioners who were appointed to investigate the penitentiaries. My hon. friend nods assent. I have read over that report, and I notice that it suggests certain amendments which are quite radical changes in the existing law. I would suggest to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister that unless we are going to fix a date in June to discuss this Bill, together with the Bill amending the Criminal Code, we might better discuss
it next session. The Bill might be printed, so that hon. members could familiarize themselves with it. It is a long and important Bill, and as we are trying to get away by next Saturday I do not think it is fair that we should be called upon to make a study of this important matter at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When the Bill is
printed and distributed I think it will be found that it does not involve anything so drastic as the hon. gentleman seems to apprehend.

I did not say drastic;
I said radical. There is quite a difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I might perhaps point out that the intention is to make it possible to carry out the recommendations that are made, but I do not think that there is anything that makes it imperative that they should be carried out. However, the Bill will be printed, and I shall be glad to confer with the hon. member and other hon. gentlemen. Certainly I do not want to press any legislation through without proper opportunity for its consideration. On the other hand, there are some improvements which are perhaps of a pressing nature, and possibly they might be dealt with.

speechtext: PRIVILEGE-Mr. TURGEON On the Orders of the Day:

I rise to a question of privilege. In the correspondence that the right hon. the Prime Minister read yesterday from a Conservative friend in St. John with reference to the Hon. Mr. Veniot, Minister of Public Works in the New Brunswick Cabinet, a reference is made to me which I cannot allow to pass unnoticed. In his letter he says:
Of course Mr. Veniot would have a portfolio In Cabinet. To make an opening for him Mr. Turgeon would have to be provided for and Mr. Veniot for the time being, at least, represent Gloucester.
Let me say that Mr. Turgeon is well provided for by the electors of Gloucester county, and wants nobody else to provide for him. The writer in question, I am sure, was not acquainted with the mentality of the people of Gloucester when he wrote that letter. Possibly he has been better informed since.

I beg to draw the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) to a statement made in the House yesterday in reference to the list of Grand Trunk shareholders. My right hon. friend yesterday stated, as reported at page 3804 of Hansard:	'
This list has been required in connection with the Grand Trunk Arbitration proceedings, and had to be sent twice to Montreal. It is in the department at present and is available.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
What I stated to the House yesterday was based on a memo, supplied me by the Department of Railways and Canals. I find I have not that memo, in my desk at the moment, but I do not think it gave the date of arrival of the packing box containing the names, nor did it say what use was made of the material by the Arbitration Tribunal; it simply said it had . been necessary. It did not say, either, what the cost was, but I do not think it is hard to divine that the cost would be

I will endeavour to find out what the uses of the list were, when it was received, and, if I can, what the cost was, but I do not know whether that will, be in the possession of the department or not.

I ask the date for the reason that my right hon. friend, when he answered me two days ago, said he was not aware that the list had arrived, and yesterday he informed the House that it had gone to Montreal in connection with the Grand Trunk arbitration proceedings which took place a month ago.

arrived until I got this memorandum from the Department of Railways and Canals.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's) :
speechtext: May I call the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), to Order No. 38 with respect to the Supplementary Extradition Convention Treaty with the United States of America? Is there any correspondence on this subject and will the right hon. minister be good enough to bring it down before the measure is proceeded with?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe some correspondence has been exchanged with the persons who are interested in the Treaty, and I shall be glad to bring it down.
That is, correspondence in connection with any action taken by the Government in reference to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will look into the
matter. Perhaps I might say now that in view of the report of the proceedings of the Senate laid on the table to-day, it will be necessary for us to drop the proposed Bill for the present. It appeared by the report, when we received it, that the message from the Embassy in Washington was erroneous in that it informed us that the Senate had ratified the Treaty, whereas we find, from the documents that have come to hand, that their ratification was subject to an amendment which very substantially modifies the convention. Of course, that amendment would have to be agreed to by the other contracting party before there could be a treaty which would

be susceptible of ratification, and I therefore propose, when the Order is called, to ask leave to withdraw the Bill.

If the Bill is not to be proceeded with, I will not, of course, trouble my right hon. friend for the present to submit any correspondence. The matter will come up at a later stage, and when it does it will be time enough to ask for the correspondence.

On the Orders of the Day:
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac) : I notice in this morning's Journal a report to the effect that Sir Joseph Flavelle, Edward G. Kelley, A. J. Mitchell, E. L. Newcombe and J. N. Dupuis have been appoirited by the Government as Grand Trunk directors. If that report is correct, for what period have these directors been appointed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The gentlemen named by my
hon. friend-I do not catch all the names, but I think the list is correct-have not been appointed by the Government, because we have not the power of appointment. To make up the required number, they have been nominated by the Government for appointment by the directors themselves upon the resignation of individual directors, which resignations are called for by the Order in Council making the nominations. The Order in Council further provides, in accordance with the Bill and the agreement, that when one retires after the other, until five have retired, and these five nominated by us have been appointed, the remaining directors shall resign. Whether the appointemnts have yet taken place, I am not certain, but the Order was cabled over the day it was passed, and I would presume that if the appointments have not taken place yet. they will very shortly. Under the statute, it was necessary that the directors be nominated by the Government, and these gentlemen are the directors so nominated. They are merely in charge until the calling into effect of the Canadian National Railway Act, upon which it is intended that the Grand Trunk shall be placed under that directorate. That is expected to take place shortly. The new directorate will take charge, and unless there is some reason to the contrary, almost immediately afterwards it is the intention to call the Act into effect.
