speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose last evening we were considering the last of the resolutions which will be found as an appendix to the Votes and Proceedings of Monday, May 9. The first, second and third of these resolutions, to amend the Special War Revenue Act, had been adopted, and the Committee was considering resolution No. 19 bbb, which had been amended by inserting the words " including rolled oats," in the ninth line on the second page, and striking out the words " when in packages weighing not less than 48 pounds each". Shall this resolution as amended, carry?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I intimated last night that there were some amendments

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
proposed to be made in the resolution and we dealt last night with one of them in connection with oatmeal in packages. The formal resolution which I desire to have adopted on that point is that the words "and oatmeal when in packages weighing not less than forty-eight pounds each" on lines 9 and 10 on page 8 of the resolutions be struck out and the following substituted therefor "oatmeal, rolled oats and corn-meal." Then there is a further change in order to remove a doubt-a doubt which arose in the discussion yesterday-having regard to the duties on spirits, as to whether or not the provinces who bought for the purposes of resale would or would not be liable to taxation. I desire to move a further resolution so as to remove all doubt in that connection. I move that the following words be added on the fifth line of page 8 of the resolution, after the word "consumers":
-including- sales to His Majesty, whether in the right of His Majesty's Government of Canada or His Majesty's Government of any province of Canada, for the purposes of resale.
I also move that, in the sixth line of the same page, the following words be added after the word "consumers":
including importations -by His Majesty, whether in the right of His Majesty's Government of Canada or His Majesty's Government of any province, for the purposes of resale.

Will the minister
kindly read the clause in its amended form?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The clause
in its amended form will read as follows:
That in addition to the present duties of customs and excise there shall be imposed, levied and collected an excise tax of one and one-half per cent on sales and deliveries toy Canadian manufacturers or producers, and wholesalers or jobbers, and a tax of two and one-half per cent on the duty paid value of the goods imported, but in respect of sales by manufacturers to retailers or consumers-
Now the addition comes in there-
- including sales to His Majesty, whether in the right of His -Majesty's Government of Canada or His Majesty's Government of any province of Canada, for the purposes of resale, the excise tax payable shall be three per cent and on goods imported by retailers or consumers, including importations by His Majesty whether in the r ght of His Majesty's Government of Canada or His Majesty's Government of any provinc, of Canada, for the purposes of resale, the excise tax payable on the duty paid value shall be four per cent.
The whole effect is to add to the operations of the Crown the tax which is put upon the general public. It follows the

principle established by . the Customs Amendment Act of 1917 and the language of that Act.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry?
Before the amendment carries I would like to ask if the minister has any statement to make in regard to what I pointed out to him last night.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend will allow me I will have great pleasure in dealing with that matter when we come to it, I have not overlooked anything.

The effect of the minister's proposition is to levy a tax upon the purchases of either the Dominion or the provinces. In the case of a tax by the Dominion it is simply a case of the money going from one pocket to the other. In the case of the provinces, however, it is either a tax upon the seller or the buyer. I do not think there has ever been any question-in practice at any rate whether there is in law-of the right of the Dominion Government to impose taxation on articles imported by the provinces. I know of cases that came up in my own province where the province has had to pay the tax. I believe there is some question now as to its legality, but in practice there has never been any hesitation on the part of the Dominion to collect taxes on goods imported by the provinces.
_ Mr. VIEN: Is there not a case in British Columbia at the present time in which this question is in dispute?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not that I
know of. From what I see in the papers, however, I believe the Attorney General of British Columbia has challenged our right to collect the increased spirit taxes from that province and the Government received a wire from him asking whether it was our intention to collect. We have so advised him.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
: If hon. gentlemen will look at the next paragraph, which deals with lumber, they will see that it is only the manufacturers' sale of lumber which carries a tax, and that there is no tax in respect of sale by the wholesaler, An amendment is proposed in that connection to make it perfectly clear that not only shall there be only one tax in the case

of domestic lumber, but that there shall also be only one tax in connection with imported lumber, which was my intention. I am therefore making a change in the basic rate. Hon. gentlemen will see that the resolution reads:
Provided that in respect ot lumber an excise tax of three per cent shall be imposed, levied-
And so on. The motion is:
That the word "two" be substituted for the word "three" in the first line of the sub-provision.
Reducing the rate.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Reducing the
rate to two per cent. And then the further addition:-

Before the minister
proceeds, may I bring to his attention a special case?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think perhaps what I am about to read will meet the hon. gentleman's case. I will be very pleased to discuss it after he has heard this motion. Then I propose this further addition :
That after the word "manufacturer" in the second line of that suh-provision, the following words be added : "and of three per cent on importation."
The sub-provision will then be in this form:
Provided that in respect of lumber an excise tax of two per cent shall be imposed, levied and collected on sales and deliveries by the Canadian manufacturer and of three per cent on importations, and that no further excise tax shall he payable on resale.

What change is there from
last year?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There were
two taxes collected on lumber last year; it is now reduced to one tax.

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a special case. It is the spirit of the law that the tax applies where a farmer brings his logs to the local saw-mill to be sawn into boards or any other form for his own use? I was told first that the tax could not be applied because there was no manufacture, and I gave that information to the newspapers so that all the farmers in my riding might be advised. Four months later I received a letter that the department had changed their mind, and then I had to advise my constituents that they would have to pay the tax.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The basis is
somewhat changed this year. We are tax-
2371	i	.i I*
ing entirely on sales. In the case my hon. friend refers to there was no sale, and therefore there would be no tax under the new law.
Do I understand the minister to say that whenever a farmer brings his logs to the mill to be sawn into boards, planks or any other form for his own use there is no tax?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is custom sawing, and there is no sale involved.

My hon. friend will remember the objection I made to the excise tax on lumber in the course of my speech on the Budget. I presented to the House at the time the difficulty of selling lumber on account of its high price, due in part to the increased freight rates, and that consequently this discouraged building and raised rents in the cities. My opinion has been strengthened by advices I have received from different parts of the country. Therefore I move, Mr. Chairman, that all of this clause referring to the excise duty on lumber be struck out.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is an exception in favour of lumber, and the effect of my hon. friend's motion would be to raise the tax to three per cent instead of two per cent, which I am sure is not what he desires. We are not increasing the tax in this instance over what it was last year.
It is increased by one and a-half per cent.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Excuse me, we are cutting it down to two per cent.
Mr. P'EDLOW: What are the special reasons for exempting the products of the forest under this clause?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That was
done for the same reason that we have made other general exemptions. The primary activities of the farms, the mines, the forests and the fisheries are absolutely exempted.

This, then, is for the benefit more particularly of the lumber interests. I was under the impression that they were in a class by themselves and well able to take care of a tax proposition of this kind; I was not aware that they were exactly in the same class as the fishermen, the farmers and the miners. I fail to apprehend why special consideration should be given to lumber-

men. They are considered wealthy people and, I should think, well able to bear an imposition of this kind.
They are not all wealthy by any means.

Would not the tax bear pretty heavily on settlers who get out their own pulpwood? That is the only means some of them have of making a livelihood in the winter time, and the tax as suggested by my hon. friend would, I think, bear pretty heavily on them.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In answer to the hon. gentleman I can very well understand his not having got the whole of this long resolution thoroughly digested. I know I have great difficulty myself in recollecting the whole of it. But I should like to point out to him that this provision only helps the primary activity; it does not help the operations of the large lumber companies, except to the extent that we are not increasing the rate on lumber by not putting the extra one-half per cent on each transaction; to that extent it may be said we are doing something for the lumber companies; but, on the other hand, there is a great deal to be said in connection with the high cost of lumber and its effect upon building operations. What are exempted are the farmers and settlers' activities, the logs they get out, round and unmanufactured timber, fence posts, railway ties, pulpwood, tan bark and other articles-the products of the forests when produced and sold by the individual settler or farmer. What we are doing, is, as I say, making all the activities of the farmer, so far as he is directly concerned, free of tax.

Then, Mr. Chairman, no ruling of the department would exempt operations by large lumbermen. That being the case, the point raised by the hon. member (Mr. Simpson) a few minutes ago regarding the taking out of pulpwood by the individual settler would be covered by this sub-provision, but it would not apply to operations by large lumber concerns?
Would this include hewn timber got out by the new settler? I have in mind unmanufactured timber- squared timber.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The qualification "unmanufactured" refers to activities of those other than farmers. Any one of the big companies to which the hon.

member for Renfrew was referring could get out their logs in the first instance without paying on them; they would pay on their lumber, not on their logs. So far as the farmer is concerned all products of the forests that he produces are free.

Will the minister explain circular No. 75C which was sent to me the other day? I was plainly told that the farmers would have to pay a tax on the amount charged for the sawing of their logs in the mill.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That, of
course, is under the old law. This new law will supersede it.
Then circular No. 75C will be got rid of?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All the old circulars will go.
Will this tax be imposed on the price f.o.b. mill or on the price at the point of delivery?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The tax is on the consideration of the sale, whatever that may be.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I wish to
move a further amendment: that in the proviso .which deals with exemptions, in the 8th line after the word "state," there be added the following words:
bran, shorts, oil oake, oil cake meal, grains mixed or crushed for poultry feed.

The minister has not included cattle feed. I would point out that more grain mixed and crushed is sold for cattle feed than is sold for poultry feed. According to the amendment, the exemption would apply only to grains mixed or crushed for poultry feed.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thought I
had made it clear; my intention is to do just what the hon. gentleman has in mind. If there is any doubt about it, the words "cattle or" may be added before the words "poultry feed."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
"Grains mixed or
crushed for cattle or poultry feed".

If it is the intention to include all feeds that are sold as cattle feed, I would point out that the minister is discriminating against certain kinds of feed that are made in this country-gluten feed, for instance, distillers' grain and brewers' grain. These are all sold quite extensively for cattle feed,

I do not rise to offer any particular objection, but there is an evident discrimination here.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid we cannot go further; we have gone as far as possible to look after the real essentials. We are not thinking of patent feeds or manufacturers' names, or anything of that kind. I will not say for a moment that it is possible to provide for every single contingency that might arise in connection with this taxation-it cannot be done.
It may be that in this discussion something else may be found which properly, economically ought to be exempt, and power is reserved to the Governor in Council to make further and other exemptions should occasion require that.

I am
quite willing that the minister should get after those compounds to which he refers as patent foods; but gluten meal is a byproduct of the starch factories; it is in the same class as oil cake or oil cake meal.
Has the minister been able to give any attention to the point that I raised, whether he should not include in [DOT] the list of exemptions the manufacture of small boats, coastal or fishing boats.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a matter that I am entirely in sympathy with, but it is a little difficult to work it out. I gave instructions for a resolution to be drawn. I have not been able to get the proper, definite information which will enable us clearly to carry out what the hon. gentleman desires to have done. It is a matter which will be taken care of at the first possible minute by Order in Council.

If I have the word of the minister that sales of these boats will be exempt and that the manufacturer of these boats is not to be taxed, or required to take out a license, I am satisfied. 1 notice that I am reported in Hansard as saying that on that subject I have had trouble with the department. That is hardly correct. I have had no trouble with the department. I have had to trouble the department occasionally with cases of this kind, but in every case I have received every attention and courtesy from the department, and I was not intending to complain of it.

I intended to speak of the point brought up by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) regarding fishing boats, and also the section of the clause which reads:
Ships licensed to engage in the Canadian coastal trade.
It seems to me that it would be only right and proper that, not only ships engaged in coastal trade, but ships engaged in fishing, should be exempted. The easiest way to get over the difficulty with regard to both fishing vessels and coastal boats would be to make that part of the clause read:
Ships and boats engaged in the Canadian coastal and fishing trade.
The minister will see in a moment that it is more important to have fishing vessels exempted than even coastal vessels. As regards the previous phrase:
Materials for use only in the construction, equipment and repair of ships.
I would suggest that in order to include the fishing industry, which is one of the basic industries of the country, that might very well read:
Materials for use only in the construction, equipment and repair of ships and fishing boats.
In justice to this great industry and to encourage it, fishing boats should be included in the list of exemptions.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will certainly go very carefully into the matter with a view of defining it.

A fishing vessel, I
imagine, would be held to be a coastal vessel.
No.

A vessel when she is not catching fish is apt to carry a cargo along the coast. I quite agree, however, with the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) that if there is any doubt about the matter, it is well to have it defined.

What action has the minister taken regarding this paragraph:
Materials for use solely in the manufacture of oleomargarine or any substitute for butter or lard or for the production of cottolene.
The minister must be well aware that the price of butter in Canada to-day is down to the pre-war rate and even below it. If you are to allow to enter Canada all kinds of material for the manufacture of these articles, then to allow the manufacturers to take the butter produced by the farmer and mix it with their different materials, and then allow the product to go

on sale in opposition to the sale of butter, I cannot help thinking that, to say the least, you are interfering with the dairy market. Has the minister seriously considered the question of placing a duty on materials that are coming into Canada for the manufacture of butter substitutes?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Had we not better adopt the amendment before we discuss the question of oleomargarine?

Before the amendment is adopted, I would like to point out to the minister that I am ready to support him in this, that I think it is good legislation to exempt the' cattle feeds that he has enumerated; but if he exempts cottonseed and oil cake meal, there is no reason why he should not exempt gluten meal, which is also used on the farm.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have
taken power to. give further exemptions, and that matter will be carefully looked into.

It is
difficult to find out just what is intended by amendments which we have never seen and which we merely hear discussed back and forth. I understand the minister is including in exemptions, brans, shorts and certain crushed feed. I caught the expression "mixed grain."

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Crushed
grains.
Crushed grains of any kind. Grain unmixed with crushed grain would be exempt.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All grains
were exempt. The term "crushed grains" was put in just to make the matter absolutely sure.

With reference to cottonseed meal and oil cake, I think they come under the same head as gluten meal, but I think they all ought to pay the sales tax and not be exempted. They are after all manufactured goods. Bran and shorts are by-products.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Mr. HAROLD- While we are on the discussion of additions to this list of goods to be exempted from this tax, I should like to bring before the committee, for the consideration of the Minister of Finance, a question that was brought up last year, namely the exemption of fibre, for us only in the manufacture of binder twine. We discussed that very fully last year, and it

was put on the free list. I think, through a misunderstanding, it was left off this year, and the way in which the matter works out under the regulations as they are now proposed, is that the Canadian manufacturer has to pay a 2i pei cent import duty on his raw materials Then when he ships his goods out to the retailer, he has to pay 3 per cent under the retail tax, or, all told, 5i per cent; whereas the United States manufacturer shipping his goods in here direct to the retailer has to pay only 4 per cent of an import duty. That leaves the Canadian manufacturer with a handicap of 1J per cent, as the finished goods come in free. The Canadian manufacturer has fixed his price for the- season, and he has based his cost upon the cost of these materials free from this tax. If he is compelled to pay it, it will certainly be a very serious thing for him, and it may result in a loss	on his season's operations.
The reason I feel that it should come up now and not be left until after this Bill has passed is in order to avoid raising the difficult question with regard to rebate on any material that has been imported. I have a letter from one manufacturer in which he says that he has paid duty already on one shipment amounting to nearly $600. I do not see how anybody can object to this change as it is with respect to an industry that is without a particle of protection. It is in one sense a great handicap from the fact that it has to pay taxes in this country while competing with the output of large concerns on the other side which contribute absolutely nothing to the treasury except this import tax. The matter was gone into very fully last year, and the minister, realizing the situation, made this alteration. So far as the farmers are concerned, this could not help but tend towards being a benefit to them, because if the thx remains on, the Canadian manufacturer would certainly have to add that tax on his raw material to the price of his finished product, if he could get the price. I do not think that any person can reasonably object to this action on the part of the Government.

I would like to join
my voice to that of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Harold) in his request. We have a large institution manufacturing binder twine in the city of Brantford, employing a large number of hands, and with a good deal of farmers' capital invested in the enterprise. It is working under absolutely free trade conditions, and I cannot

imagine that any one in this House would ask that a business that is without any protection whatever should be placed under a handicap as compared with the competition that it has to meet from the south of the line. This industry has had a difficult career, but has managed to weather the storm with absolute free trade in that particular article, through success in its purchasing of raw material and the great deal of foresight that has been exercised by the management for a great many years.
I do trust that the Minister of Finance will give the request of the hon. member for Brant his very serious consideration, because I cannot imagine that anybody would wish to place an extra 11 per cent on an article in such universal use as this, on which the margin of profit is small, and which is an industry that it is very desirable should be maintained in Canada. There are only three factories left in Canada manufacturing binder twine, and I hope the minister will see his way clear to grant this small concession with respect to the raw material entering into the manufacturing of binder twine.

I would like to direct
the attention of the House to one fact that has been brought out by the hon. member ' for Brantford, and that is that all that is necessary to make a success of a Canadian factory is good management, plus free trade. I am delighted to know that the hon. member for Brantford is a convert to that idea.

I appreciate the
difficulties of the Minister of Finance in securing revenues to meet our obligations. I do think, however, that there are some industries in this country that ought to fc encouraged 'as much as possible, and consequently I quite agree with the exception that has been taken by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong). In connection with the articles which are being exempted, particularly importations into this country of cream, butter, cheese, oleomargarine, margarine, butterine or other substitutes for butter, eggs, vegetables, fruits, grains and so forth, I think we all realize that there is altogether too much of our money being paid to the United States for products that we could very well raise in this country. That was more noticeable during the last month perhaps than at any other time. As the result of the tremendous importations from the United States, one of these articles- butter-has dropped 25 cents a pound in price in one week. I have here a publication of the Department of Agriculture giving importations for the month of March and I find that there were 753,726 pounds of butter, and 374,672 pounds of oleomargarine imported in that month, and that the total of dairy products imported was 1,607,741 pounds. Our money was paid out to the United States for this stuff at a time when we were looking for markets abroad for our own produce.
While dealing with this matter, I might point out that it has engaged the attention of the House on quite a number of occasions. My hon. friend from East Lambton has mentioned the exemption with respect to materials for use solely in the manufac-ure of oleomargarine or any substitute for butter, or lard, or for the production of cottolene. It is somewhat interesting to note how many of these different ingredients are used by the manufacturers of oleomargarine, who are carrying on this business of the adulteration of butter. Their business is not the manufacturing of oleomargarine at all, but the adulteration of butter. I would not take any exception to importing margarine into this country and manufacturing it, but what I do object to, and have objected to all along, is permitting these manufacturers to adulterate butter, which is the right that has been given to them under the regulations under which they are carrying on. There are two manufacturers in Canada, both in Ontario, engaged in this business. We are told that there have been circulars issued by them and by other associations to every member of the House pointing out that it was a Canadian product that was being used to adulterate butter, and that consequently the manufacture of oleomargarine was to the advantage of some branch of agriculture in Canada, particularly oleo oil.
What is the real situation? For the eleven months of the past year, the latest returns that I have, oleo oils were imported into this country to the extent of 1,714,562 pounds, for the purpose of adulterating butter. Cotton seed oil was imported to the amount of 889,208 pounds. These importations together with those of salt, stearine, butter oil, peanut oil, corn oil, cocoanut oil, aggregated 3,680,350 pounds. Now there is a desire on the part of the Government and of every one else to encourage Canadian manufacturers and Canadian producers. I want to point out that 99 per cent of the duty paid on these articles in the past year has been rebated to these two manufacturers, or an amount of $138,367.34. I think that instead of

exempting the importation of this stuff from any tax, as we are doing in this resolution, we should endeavour to protect and encourage our own industries. There has been dumped on the markets of this country during the past three months immense quantities of dairy products from Denmark, Holland, the Argentine, and the United States, of a very inferior quality. This stuff was churned in the churns of certain manufacturers in the city of Toronto, and placed on the market because it had very little value as it was. This is the sort of thing that has been going on for some time. We speak about the need for protection. If ever there was a time in the history of this country when the dairying industry needed some consideration and encouragement, it is now. I think we should be well advised, not only in putting a tax on the imports, hut also in increasing the protective tariff against these inferior articles which have been brought into this country to such a large extent during the last few months. I have repeatedly pointed out the effect of this matter. The great objection is that we are exempting articles that are being brought in and used by the manufacturers to adulterate butter. That is really what the business is; they are not really manufacturing oleomargarine at all. What does adulteration mean? It means the mixing of base materials with something superior, and that is the very thing that the manufacturers of oleomargarine are doing. The manufacturers of butter are prevented from doing anything of that kind because they are surrounded with regulations, municipal, provincial and federal. These regulations are designed to ensure the purity of butter, and we immediately discard all these provisions and permit certain manufacturers to get a license to buy that article by millions of pounds and adulterate it with these inferior commodities. It is the purpose of this 'schedule to permit that stuff to come in without being taxed, I think we should place a heavy tax on such importations introduced for the purpose of adulterating good food.

I endorse what has been said by the three last speakers. We are dealing with two specific articles in connection with which some consideration should he given the industries concerned. As regards binder twine, the present arrangement will have two effects. It will place the manufacturer of this article in 
Canada at a disadvantage, as compared with the American manufacturer, and as a result the cost will be increased to the consumer, and the farmer will be affected. I think, therefore, that some consideration should be given that point. I am in perfect accord with the views expressed by the last speaker (Mr. Sutherland) . A year ago, perhaps, I would not have taken this position, when butter was selling at 75 cents, 80 cents, 85 and 90 cents a pound. The poorer people of the country were in such a position that a strong argument could be advanced for giving them a cheaper article to take the place of butter. But with butter at its present price-and the probability is that it will be lower instead of higher-there is a great deal of force in what my hon. friend from South Oxford has said.
I regret to have to ask the committee to revert to a former item, but I want to ask the minister a question with regard to cord wood used for fuel purposes.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All fuel is
free.
Then my question is not necessary.

I would impress upon the minister the importance of a sane and logical position when we are protecting industries. We are protecting nearly every industry, because we are a protective country, and yet we foolishly allow one of the greatest industries to go unprotected. That is not sound or logical, nor is it in the interests of Canada. As I said the other night, we might very well, at this time, take a lesson from the United States. We know what they are doing to protect the farmers of that country, and we are not so foolish as to believe that their action will not have some effect on this country.
I would therefore impress upon the Government the necessity of giving to the farmers of Canada some protection along these lines.

I support the last speaker. In British Columbia, under present conditions, our farmers are very much in need of some protection. The other day I received a letter-I notice some of the Agrarians smiling-from a branch of the United Farmers of British Columbia. I am sorry I have not that letter here; it is in my room, but I will bring it down

later. It was accompanied by a copy of a resolution passed at a meeting of the Surrey and Barnston Island branch of the United Farmers of British Columbia, urging very strongly that some extra measure of protection be provided the farmers of that province, and mentioning particularly butter, poultry, eggs, and other farm produce of that kind.
What about tobacco?
It is also stated that the market was being flooded with American goods.
Reciprocity.

Personally, I am quite familiar with the condition which prevails in that province, and I know that our farmers are suffering very severely.
I do not think the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), will have very much support out in that country for the doctrine he is preaching in the Prairie Provinces. It may be that our conditions are peculiar in some ways, inasmuch as the markets of Westminister and Vancouver are situated so close to the boundary line, and are the best markets for the northern part of the state of Washington. Now, the farmers in Washington are shipping in by truckloads large quantities of all kinds of produce, and as they have the benefit of several weeks in the matter of time, they can send in their goods before the farmers in our part of the country can put their produce on the market, and therefore they have a much more favourable market than our people can find later on. I am very glad the subject has been mentioned, and I hope the minister will give this matter his very serious consideration. I am sure I speak for the great majority of the farmers of British Columbia when I say they want protection, and still more protection.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have in my hand a table of the importations of butter into Canada. I have been trying to follow weekly, and sometimes daily, these importations. At the present time we want to keep as much money at home for Canada as we can, and 1 have therefore been interested in this matter. I happened to have this list in my pocket, and it will probably be interesting to say what the imports actually are. Of course, there is practically nothing from the United Kingdom; the imports of butter for the fiscal year amounted to 112 pounds. There
was practically nothing from Newfoundland, the imports amounting to 1,049 lbs. New Zealand, on the other hand had a good deal larger export to Canada; she sold us 1,533,280 lbs. Holland sold us only 110 lbs., but our imports from the United States amounted to 2,207,077 lbs. These are the figures for the past fiscal year ending March 31. The figures for the month of April last show an importa-tation from New Zealand of 90,776 lbs., and from the United States, 576,061 lbs. It will be observed that the importations of butter from the United States for the whole of the previous year were 2,200,000 pounds of butter and for last month, 576,061 pounds, showing a large increase in American importations. Now there is a duty of four cents a pound on butter, but I am afraid we cannot very well discuss protection or the tariff on the sales tax, and however one may sympathize, and ought to sympathize, with the dairymen this is not the time for us to consider that matter. There is still on the Order Paper an oleomargarine resolution in connection with which that matter might properly be discussed, but I am afraid we cannot take it up in connection with this sales tax resolution.

It is pleasing to know that in the calm and agreeable atmosphere of the last day or two some light has been coming to hon. gentlemen opposite, including my hon. friend from Brantford. Hon. gentlemen opposite have within the past twenty-four hours voted that they do not want any tariff revision, and now they are giving us many reasons why the tariff ought to be revised.

The exception I take to the exemption from taxation of butter importations into this country is, I contend, a legitimate matter to discuss in connection with this resolution, which specifically mentions the importations which shall be exempt from the tax we propose to place on other articles. With reference to the importations of butter I am a little surprised that they do not amount to more than the figures given by the minister of 576,061 pounds for the month of April. Could the minister give us the importations for the month of March?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They would be included in the total of the two millions odd for the year.

1 have here a copy of the report which is sent to mem-

hers from the Markets Division of the Dairy and Cold Storage Branch of the Department of Agriculture and it gives the importations into Canada from the United States of dairy products and oleomargarine. Why they should include oleomargarine with dairy products is beyond my comprehension. In France the retailer is not permitted tc sell the two articles, yet you find it included with butter in the market reports of the Dairy and Cold Storage Branch of the Canadian Department of Agriculture. According to the report in question the following importations from the United States were made in the month
of March:
Lbs.
Butter	 753,726
Cheese	 64,243
Condensed milk	 7,200
Evaporated milk	 240
Buttermilk	 7,660
Oleomargarine	 374,672
Total	 1,207,741
Now that is quite a large quantity of this stuff to be dumped into this country during one month and the effect of it, as I have already pointed out, is that the market for butter broke to the extent of over twenty-five cents a pound in one week, and I fear that before three months are over the price will be very much lower than it is to-day. Although the people in the constituency which I have the honour to represent are not much interested in the butter making industry, yet I fully appreciate the importance of butter making to this country. I believe it is really the foundation of the live stock industry of Canada. You may manufacture cheese, condense milk, buttermilk, or other things, but in so doing you get away from the real live stock business of the country. You cannot afford to feed whole milk in order to raise young stock because it is altogether too expensive. Therefore butter making, to my mind, is the most important and most essential branch of agriculture we have in the Dominion. If we are going to maintain that industry we must increase the fertility of our soil and pay more attention to the live stock industry. The butter making which is carried on in some other parts of the country, in my opinion is the most important of all, I would strongly recommend that when the proper time comes the present duty should be increased. In the meantime I would impose a tax upon the importation of all the articles mentioned that are coming into this country, and in particular on the ingredients that go into the manufacture of oleomargarine.

The hon. member has half a dozen times used the expression that millions of pounds of butter are being "dumped into Canada." Now dumping has a technical meaning, we have a law against dumping, and if my hon. friend is correct that these goods have been "dumped" into Canada he has made a very serious reflection upon the Department of Customs. I do not think he is correct, I am willing to believe that the Department of Customs is enforcing the anti-dumping law. When the hon. gentleman uses the word "dumping" he is doubtless using it in the broad sense that a large quantity of the goods to which he refers has been imported. I take it for granted he is correct in that, but when he says these goods have been dumped into Canada I think perhaps, it expresses a meaning beyond what my hon. friend intended.

Does my hon. friend
want a sales tax put on eggs? Of course, it is the sales tax we are dealing with.
I am speaking on a matter that was brought up by several hon. gentlemen who suggested that some kind of customs duty should be imposed on foreign produce.
We cannot do that here.
Each egg would have to be branded under the law before being imported.
It is going to be arranged so the hen does that.

I would suggest that the Minister of Finance supply the hens interested with a rubber stamp attachment.
Mr, FIELDING: I did not want to raise a point of order against my hon. friend
from New Westminster so I allowed him to read his letter. But evidently he has made a mistake. He should have produced this in the Budget debate before he voted that the tariff was right.
We have spent two full weeks' discussing free trade and protection, but our high protectionist friends on the other side do not seem to be satisfied yet.
Do not let us prolong the Budget discussion.

As my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's has said, they did not want to revise the tariff, but now apparently they are bent on revising it. They did not vote properly the other day; they made a mistake, as they admit themselves, and should have voted on the other side. There may be some farmers throughout the Dominion who are anxious to raise their prices by protection so that the unemployed workingmen may have to pay more for their food, but our farmers generally want protection only from the protected interests. We have had some remarks made that should receive consideration, and it seems to me that these other things are thrown into distract attention. I should like to know from the minister whether there is anything in the point raised by my hon. friend from Brant. I do not know that I grasped exactly the way in which he suggested that our manufacturers of binder twine would have to pay one and a half cent more than the importer. If there is anything in that I think it should receive attention.	^

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would submit, Mr. Chairman, that we will have to consider any further tariff discussion on this sales tax as out of order.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe there is a great deal in the point raised by the hon. member for Brant, and I agree very largely with what he has said. I shall have the same pleasure in taking it up as I shall have in considering what my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's suggested in connection with fishing boats, with a view to taking action.

The minister has promised
to reconsider the tax on the lumber interests. May I suggest in that connection that he take into consideration this feature?

If it is desirable to exempt from the sales tax lumber that goes into the construction of ships, would it not be well to reconsider upon what basis we should tax lumber going into the construction of houses, harns and stables ?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a
further amendment I wish to move before the clause is adopted, Mr. Chairman, and although it is fairly long it is very simple. Before the basis of taxation was arrived at and adopted submissions were received as to the best methods of raising the required revenue from witnesses in every walk of life, from boards of trade and kindred commercial associations and from farmers' institutes who appeared before the Tariff Commission. One of the things which was urged from time to time was the general turnover tax, and in that connection the desire was expressed that book-keeping troubles should be saved and that the tax should not be shown separately upon the invoice. Since the resolution has been brought down on looking further into the matter and having particular regard to the question of checking revenues, we have come to the conclusion that we had better stick to the law as we had it before. Taking that course, I move:
That the following words be added after the word "cent" on third line of page 8 of Resolutions :
"that the purchaser shall be furnished with a written invoice of any sale, which invoice shall state separately the amount of such tax to at least the extent of one and one-half per cent but such tax must not be included in the manufacturer's, producer's or wholesaler's costs on which profit is calculated; and the tax ishall be payable iby 'the purchaser to the wholesaler, producer or manufacturer at the time of such sale, and by the wholesaler, producer or manufacturer to His Majesty in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed, and such wholesaler, producer or manufacturer shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred dollars, if such payments are not made, and in addition shall be liable to a penalty equal to double the amount of the excise duties unpaid; that the term "duty paid value" means the value of the article as it would be determined for the purpose of calculating an ad valorem duty upon the importation of same into Canada under the laws relating to the Customs and the Customs Tariff whether such article be in fact subject to ad valorem or other duty or not, and in addition the amount of the Customs duties, if any, payable thereon".

I have in my hand a clipping from the Ottawa Journal of May 13, 1921, which reads as follows:
Wholesalers oppose the Sales Tax Change

Want Levy Shown Separately on the Invoices.
Montreal, May 17.-In connection with protests against the proposals of the Minister of

Finance, as outlined in the Budget, the branches of the local Board of Trade have been busy passing resolutions of dissatisfaction and forwarding them to Sir Henry Drayton. In addition to the Wholesale Grocers' Guild and the Produce Merchants' Association, the Montreal Wholesale Drygoods Association held a meeting to-day, and adopted a resolution supporting the principle of setting out on the invoice the amount of sales tax, apart from the costs, and directed their secretary to send copies of this resolution to the drygoods sections of the Boards of Trade of Toronto, Winnipeg, Quebec and Halifax for further consideration and action. A meeting of the lumber association to consider similar questions will be held here to-morrow.
It would appear that this change has been made in response to the protests received from the sources indicated in this despatch. Now, I 'am distinctly opposed to this change. I may be out of harmony with the wishes of the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada, just as I was out of harmony a year ago with the resolution presented to the Minister of Finance by that association. If the minister had listened to the suggestions which I made then, he would not only have saved himself a considerable amount of trouble but he would have saved the retail trade of this country an enormous amount of worry, annoyance and dissatisfaction. The statement which I made on that occasion will be found on page 3341 of Hansard, session of 1920, volume 4. On that occasion I said:
The Minister of Finance has decided on a certain method of collecting these taxes. It does not meet with my approval and I would suggest some other method, tout he is the man in charge of the ship and he is responsible.
Further on I said:
We have to raise the money, and if the Minister of Finance has decided that this is the best way in which to raise it, we have no alternative but to submit and try it out.
Further on in the discussion I said:
I should like to persuade him to try another method, but I understand that is impossible.
I may add that during that discussion I quoted from a resolution presented to the minister by the Retail Merchants' Association, drygoods section, endorsing the principle of collecting the revenue through the medium of the luxury tax. This resolution had been endorsed by the association and presented to the minister on the occasion of a meeting with him at the Chateau Laurier. Now, the House had scarcely prorogued after the session of 1920 when protests started to come in from all directions, and from that day until the luxury tax was abolished in December the minister must have had an interesting time

[DOT]of it because of the protests which came from all parts of Canada. I believed then that for an emergency the collection of a sales tax would be the best way of raising revenue. My suggestion then, as it is today, was the placing of a one per cent sales tax on each turnover. The present proposal is too involved: there is a one and one-half per cent tax on turn-
5 p.m. over from manufacturer and wholesaler to retailer; a two and one-half per cent tax on sales direct from the manufacturer to the retailer or consumer, a three per cent tax along another line, and, in addition, a four per cent tax on goods imported direct by retailer or consumer. Now, this will entail a great deal of checking and an enormous amount of work on the part of the importer as well as on the part of the Inland Revenue Department. If a simple tax of one per cent had been levied by the minister on each turnover he would have received as much money from the consumer, who in the final analysis must pay this tax-in fact he might have received more. I further want to go on record as favouring the principle of collecting this tax from the seller on each turnover. The principle adopted in this resolution means that the purchaser, not the seller, will have to pay the tax in each case. In my judgment the method I propose would simplify the whole system of collection and produce the returns aimed at by the Budget. I notice that in his Budget the minister has made a statement with regard to the retail trade in this country which in my judgment is not a fair statement, although I am sure the minister did not wish to be unfair to any section of the community. Here is what he said, as it appears on page 15 of the copies of the Budget speech which have been printed and distributed:
In practical administration, though, in view of the fact that after careful survey it has been established that books are not kept in many retail stores-*
I have discussed this subject with many of the men who are doing field work for the Income Tax Department, and while they admit that some retail merchants do not keep a set of books by double entry or by some other approved system, still there is hardly one that they meet in their entire travels, that does not keep a record of his sales. I should like the minister to bear that point in mind. Therefore if you establish a sales tax, you have no difficulty about a man keeping a record of his sales, so that the difficulty suggested my this statement
is not as great as it would seem if looked at from the viewpoint from which the minister looked at it. If I am correct-and I honestly believe I am-that a very small minority of those carrying on retail businesses of one class or another will be found who do not keep records of their sales, it should be a simple matter to collect a revenue on the basis of a sales or turnover tax. I am informed by very intelligent men in the service of the Income Tax Department that this is the only basis upon which, in many cases, they are able to work out an income tax return. Therefore, if they are able to work out an income tax on the basis of the record of sales of merchants, it should be a very simple matter for the department to collect a sales tax of one per cent on the turnover. A turnover tax of one per cent would be paid, in the first instance, by the importer or manufacturer, then a turnover tax of one per cent by the wholesaler or jobber, and, last, a turnover tax of one per cent by the retailer or distributor. I know a system of that kind is and has been in operation since 1905 in the Philippine Islands, and they collect a turnover tax along the lines that I suggest, but they make it apply rather from a certain amount of sales or turnover upwards. That is to say, a firm doing a certain amount of business during the year is exempted or is not bothered with, because the amount is too small; they do not look to firms of that kind for a sales tax. I feel satisfied, since the minister has committed himself to the proposition, that, as last year, he will go on with it; but I can assure him now, as I assured him a year ago, that he will have no end of difficulty, and that the men in the retail merchants' associations who are at present supporting him will be the first ones to turn round on him before the year has progressed very far.

Shall
the amendment carry?
The minister promised some consideration to the different lumber items.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I said that I
would consider the matter just as I am considering what was urged by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) in regard to boats.

As regards the question of the amendment which my hon. friend has moved, I can understand the argument that the tax, whatever it might

be, should be shown on the invoice. Whether that is wise or not, is a matter to be argued. But if a tax is to be shown, the actual tax should be shown. The taxes are 14, 24, 3 and 4 per cent, while according to the amendment moved by the minister, no tax except the one of 14 per cent shall be shown on the invoice. If any reference is to be made to the tax, why should the whole tax not be shown?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This follows the principle of last year. 'One-half of the tax may be absorbed; the rest of it must be shown.

The fact that a thing was done last year is not conclusive that it is wise. Why not show the real tax? why are the people to be deceived by the exhibition on the invoice of a tax of 14 per cent, when the real tax is 4 per cent?

The real reason for that is that the wholesaler charges the retailer li per cent, and a manufacturer shipping directly to a retailer wants the privilege of being able to charge exactly the same rate as the wholesaler. The invoice bears the same rate; but when it comes to a matter of putting on the sales tax, the jobber has the advantage in so far as he can show on the invoice a tax of only 14 per cent. That is the reason why this method was adopted, and it has worked out quite satisfactorily. I believe, if the matter is left in the way in which the minister has it, it will continue to work out all right. In my experience, I do not remember seeing an invoice on which the actual amount of the tax was not shown; but there may be instances where a business is figured very closely, and where the manufacturer or the original producer may wish to have that privilege of selling as cheaply as the wholesaler.

I have difficulty in understanding why the actual tax is not to be shown. If there is any point in showing the tax on the invoice, the whole tax should be shown. The matter may have been discussed last year, and it may have escaped my memory. What the hon. member (Mr. Harold) says is that the manufacturer or dealer may not wish it to be known what the tax really is. I do not think that is a good reason. If there are good reasons why the tax should be shown on the invoice, the statement should be an honest one as regards the tax that is paid.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The whole
idea of it is that we ape trying to deal 
fairly with both classes of business activities. There are manufacturers and wholesalers. Some manufacturers sell directly; some iise wholesalers. If a manufacturer was obliged to show the whole of the tax on the invoice, he would be showing a tax twice as great as that which the wholesaler has the right to show. The transaction is entirely with people who understand the business; this is not a question of dealing with the public at all as there is no tax upon sales from the retailer. This is merely in the trade, and it enables manufacturers to sell directly if they so desire without selling through middlemen, allowing them to pay, at their own expense, part of the tax which they are not showing.

Certain commodities are
exempt from taxation. Let us say that a mill is turning out cement. Cement is exempt, is it not?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Flour is exempt. Supposing a car of 500 bags of flour is going out. The approximate value of that at present would be $2,500; but there is a tax on the container, and the mill, under this proposed amendment, will be compelled to show 14 per cent on the invoice. That at the value of bags to-day would represent approximately 75 cents. I am satisfied that flour millers will not object to pay the tax; but would it not be more economical if they were to pay it when they buy the bags? Why compel a mill to keep a bookkeeper to look after this, because it will require practically a special man to look after and total this all up, and it will involve additional expense upon the department to look after it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is entirely
optional with the miller what he does. He may sell containers or he may not. The usual way of doing business is to make a lump charge for your commodity.
Including the bags?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and in that case there is no' tax on it. If the miller is going to make a separate charge for a container, there is a tax.
The minister rules that it is not necessary that the miller should show this tax on his invoice.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not in the flour business.

Not unless he charges for the containers. If you invoice me a carload of bran, you invoice me that at a certain price per ton; you do not charge for the bags separately. If you do it in that way there is no percentage charge.
I understood from the minister's statement a moment ago that as regards anything on which there was a tax, the man must show the tax on the invoice.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It depends
upon the sale in each case.

He pays his sales tax
when he receives the bags to the fellow who makes them, but he absorbs that tax.

I notice that
cream, butter, cheese, milk and so forth are mentioned in the amendment, but not condensed milk, or powdered milk. Might not those be included?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will consider that.	-

:	I think it is hardly fair
for the minister to patch up this resolution in the way he is doing by amendment after amendment of which no notice has been given. I have been trying to get a copy of the last amendment, but have not been able to do so, and even if I should receive a copy, it would be difficult at this moment to discuss it intelligently without having seen it before. I have no doubt the minister is acting in good faith, but I do not think he is doing justice to the committee in bringing forward amendments in this way. Copies of the amendment should have been distributed in advance.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Here is a
copy of the amendment for my hon. friend. It will be just the same method as last year.

The amendment is a long
one, of twenty-five lines. How can an hon. member express an opinion on such an important amendment that he now sees for the first time? I shall have to discuss the amendment as I understand it at the moment, but I say that it is not fair to the committee. If I understand the amendment rightly, we are reverting to the method of last year in collecting the tax.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will be the same plan as last year.

In the Budget the minister proposed a different plan from that of last year, but now he is going to revert to the method of last year. What about the
public and the trade who are interested in this Bill, and who have been informed by. the minister in his Budget speech that the plan of collection is going to be changed, and that the tax would be imposed at the point of production and the point of entry. Now the minister comes along and changes his plan altogether. I must say that I am not favourable to this sales tax, but apart from the principle, I was favourable to the method of collection which was announced by the minister in his Budget this year. Now he says that that method will not be adopted, but that he will revert to the plan of last year. I have nothing more to say at the moment, except that it is not fair to the committee or the trade and the public generally to change the method and pass the resolution without any more notice than has been given this afternoon.

I read an extract from
the Ottawa Journal a few moments ago, and I intended to make some further comments on that feature of the situation. In my judgment the minister has made this change in order to comply with the requests of the wholesale trade, the manufacturers, and other big interests in Montreal. Just a few days prior to the day on which the item I read appeared, there was another item in the press to the effect that the wholesale trade were at logger-heads regarding the collection of this tax, that some of them were absorbing it, and others were not. They were using the tax as a lever for inducing business. In order to combine upon a plan, all those interested in this matter met together and forwarded resolutions to the Minister of Finance. It would seem to me in view of the decision arrived at now, and in view of this amendment providing that the method of collection shall be the same as last year, that the minister has decided-shall I say?-to pull the chestnuts out of the fire for the wholesalers and manufacturers .of the country. That is, in my judgment, the real reason for the decision that has been arrived at.	'

The first clause says:
Provided also that the taxes specified in this section shall not apply to sales or importations of,

Bread;-flour and oatmeal, when In packages weighing not less than forty-eight pounds each;
My interpretation of that is that all flour put up in packages of forty-eight pounds and over is exempt.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That has all been struck out.
All flour is exempt?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

There is another matter. I want a ruling as to where this tax will apply on lumber or any of these other articles. Will it apply at the point of shipment or at the point of delivery? I think it is important that the country should have a ruling on that at once, because it will make a material difference to the general trade of the country.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The same
practice will be followed as in fixing valuations of imports. It entirely depends on the invoices.

Coming back to this matter I spoke of before, I could not hear the minister when he was making his statement regarding the fibre question, but I understand that he is in favour of correcting the injustice that is done under the regulations. There is one point I should like to have made clear, and that is: how will the importers stand with regard to any duties collected?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That will be quite all right.

Following up what my hon. friend from Brant has said, I notice that he brought up this same question last year. He said (Hansard, June 16, 1920, page 3623) :
Mr. Harold: Is the Minister of Finance going to add to the list of exemptions the materials and supplies that enter into the manufacture of binder twine?
Sir Henry Drayton: As the fibre which is used in the manufacture of binder twine is the important item, and as we are not adding in any way to the burdens of agriculture, I move to add to the list of exemptions after the words "heating purposes" in the amendment to paragraph (d) of resolution 7, the words "fibre for use only in the manufacture of binder twine."
I would like to ask the minister what is the objection to taking that action now?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no objection at all. As I said, I am in sympathy with it, but there are other fibre twine essentials which we have been asked to consider practically on the same grounds, and we wanted to deal with the whole matter at the same time. I cheerfully give again to my hon. friend the undertaking I have already given, that this material the hon. gentleman wants exempted will be exempted by Order in Council, and the exemption made retroactive.

Sub-section 4 exempts prayer books, hymn books, bibles, gospels,

parts of bibles. tracts, etc. Now, Catholics do not use bibles very extensively, but they do use missals and some other books of that kind. I do not see missals mentioned in this list. It may be stated that they are covered in the term "prayer books," but I think the matter should be put beyond any possibility of question.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There can be no room for question on that. Of course they are exempt. However, if my hon. friend desires any greater particularity, I do not object to adding the word "missal".

I think the word
missal ought to be added.

I suggest adding, after the word "tracts," the words "and books", 

religious tracts and books.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be too broad.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Resolution agreed to.

Before the resolution is reported, I understood that the minister had promised the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), that he would take into consideration certain exemptions in regard to lumber for ships. I also pointed out that inasmuch as he has already made provision for the exemption of lumber going into certain ships, it was an unfair discrimination to tax lumber used in the construction of houses, barns and stables. The minister promised some consideration to that matter.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The matter
brought up by the member for Shelburne and Queen's is one which will require some little consideration, in order properly to define what is to be done. I undertook that the matter would be considered by Council at an early date, and I shall be pleased at the same time to consider the question raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Robb).

Will the minister consider the advisability of including beads and crucifixes in the category of goods used in prayer, and exempting these articles? They are not used for commercial purposes, and I do not see what objection there could be to exempting them.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will also consider that in Council.

I wish to go on record
as being opposed to a tax on lumber. Lumber is a natural product of the land, and this resolution clearly establishes the

principle that natural products of the land are to be exempt. The Minister of Finance will, no doubt, say that this is true, and that he is not taxing natural products; and we find that logs and round unmanufactured timber are not to be taxed. But I would point out that lumber, even after it is sawn, is a natural product of the land, and should not be taxed, because 95 per cent of the lumber used must be sawn before anything can be done with it. I see no reason therefore why lumber should be taxed any more than products of the mines or of the sea. We must not lose sight of the fact that in Canada to-day there are half a million people without homes, and the general try at the present time is for houses, and more houses. This Parliament has voted an appropriation and has passed a law in regard to a housing scheme. Every one admits that the housing problem in Canada to-day is a most acute one, and yet we are taxing the very essential that goes to the building of the people's homes. I do not see any distinction in the resolution between the large and small saw-mill, and as between the lumber used by the small settler or farmer, and lumber used in trade and lumber sawn or manufactured for export. There are in this country any number of small mills which saw lumber for the use of the settler and the farmer, and I do not think it is right to put a tax of 3 per cent on the lumber which the farmer takes to these mills to be sawn for domestic purposes. The poorer classes are in such great need of houses to-day that nothing should be done to hamper people in building homes. The new tax should not be imposed on lumber, which is one of the principle articles used in the building of houses. At present the building trade is almost stagnant throughout the country. It was in the same state last year and the year before. What is the reason? We have come to the point where labour has decreased in certain places, and now, I am informed on very good authority, building material has also decreased 20 per cent since last year. When these other materials are being decreased I do not think it is right for the Government to impose a tax that will be burdensome to those engaged in the building trade, especially for the reason that it will tend to still furather restrict the possibility of people of the poorer classes getitng dwellings at anything like a reasonable rate. Furthermore this tax on sawn lumber is really a tax on the export lumber trade, such as is not imposed in the case of any other commodity.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is no tax on the export of lumber.
I understand that when a log has been sawn the owner of the mill is liable to a tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The tax is paid when the lumber is sold for internal consumption not for export.
I am glad to hear that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At the end of the clause there is a provision that the tax shall not be payable on goods exported.

I have one or two observations to make with regard to the sales tax. Such a tax imposed on the poor as well as on the rich is not just to the former. A sales tax of three or four per cent means practically nothing to a rich man, but such a tax on the commodities used by the poor is a very heavy burden. For that reason I am not in favour of it. I notice that in the United States Senate Senator Smoot has introduced a Bill providing for a sales tax of 1 per cent which has evoked much condemnation. Now, if a sales tax of 1 per cent in the United States is regarded as bearing heavily on the poor, what must be the effect of the imposition of a sales tax of 3 or 4 per cent in this country?

I notice there is a provision that the excise taxes specified in the section "shall not be payable on goods exported, or on sales of goods made to the order of each individual customer by a business which sells exclusively by retail." How would that operate in a case of this kind? Take a stove manufacturer who sells goods by retail all over the country. A jobber comes to his shop and says "I want 100 stoves from you and I would like my name put on those stoves." Will there be a sales tax in the case of such an order as that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Such a transaction would be covered by the regulations that will be applied under this section. My hon. friend will notice the wording "by a business which sells exclusively by retail, under regulations by the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue." Any practice of that kind would be stopped by the regulations because such is not the intention of the law. On the other hand I think the Minister of Finance has already given an illustration applicable to the case of a retail merchant. Where individuals go in and get suits of

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
clothes individually, it is not intended that the tax should apply.
Section agreed to.
Resolutions reported, read a second time and concurred in.

On motion of Right Hor.. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice) Bill No. 157 to amend the Juvenile Delinquents' Act was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On the title:

I wish to say to the Minister in connection with this Bill that there is one thing which I take exception to,-that it is to be brought into force by proclamation. This is a very inconvenient procedure and should be discouraged as much as possible. The proclamations appear in the Canada Gazette, which is read by about one-tenth of one per cent of our people, and even members of my own profession very often do not know when they read a statute that is to come into force by proclamation whether it is actually in force or not. I submit that any criminal law should come into force by the statute itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I agree on general principles with what my hon. friend said, but this is a special provision. It is not the Act itself that is to come in force on proclamation, but only one section, and that section has to do solely with the age at which, a person may be treated as a juvenile delinquent. It is not creating any new crime, it is merely providing that a larger class of boys and girls may be treated as juvenile delinquents. The special reason for taking this course is that it has been represented to us that our present reformatories-which are mostly provincial institutions-are not now prepared to take in this additional class as between the ages of 16 and 18, and that until proper ar-

rangements are made it might prove very detrimental to the younger children to be brought in contact with these older and possibly more hardened offenders. We made a similar amendment the other day to the Prisons and Reformatories' Act with the same provision. I quite recognize the force of the hon. gentleman's objection 'if this were a penal provision, but, as I have said, it applies only to a matter of procedure.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

On motion of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen (Prime Minister) Bill No. 141, to amend the Statistics Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon.-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-schedules that may be sent post free.

I have had some complaints from the Health Department of Nova Scotia which I brought to the notice of the Health Department here, and, I think, the Post Office Department also. The reports sent to Ottawa by the Provincial Health Department were formerly sent free of postage, and I understand that under the law of last year that privilege has been done away with. If we provided under this Bill that these reports might be sent free of postage, I think it would meet the public view.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Act of last year
was intended to be a relief to the Post Office
Department from a great many encumbrances on its revenue. My thought was that it was intended that these health reports should not be exempt from paying postage. The matter affected by this Bill was also last year included in the list of that not exempted, as was, indeed, everything coming from Provincial Governments. A tremendous amount of revenue was lost and all manner of stuff was sent out that was wasted simply because it
6 p.m. went free. The whole subject was reviewed, and the matter was put, as we thought, on a business basis. The hon. gentleman may possibly be light

as to the health reports, but I fancy that it is a case of services rendered the province by the Federal Government, rather than service rendered by us to the province, and they should hardly object to paying postage on them. But here we have a case where service is rendered by the provinces to us, and I understand that is why the Minister of Trade and Commerce felt he could not continue the rule of having them pay postage. Anyway, if my hon. friend were right the change would have to be made by amendment to the Health Act.
