speechtext:
On motion of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen (Prime Minister) the House went into committee to consider the following resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair: [DOT]
Resolved, That it is expedient to repeal section three of the Oleomargarine Act, 1919, chapter 24 of the statutes of 1919 (second session) as amended by section one of chapter 30 of the statutes of 1920, and to provide in lieu thereof that notwithstanding anything contained in the Dairy Industry Act, 1914, chapter seven of the statutes of 1914, or in any other statute or law, the manufacture in and importation of oleomargarine into Canada, and the offering for sale, and the having in possession for sale of oleomargarine, shall be permitted.

As representing an agricultural constituency, and having in mind the great reduction in the price of dairy products-butter and cheese-I can see no longer a necessity for the free admission of oleomargarine into this country. Formerly it was the policy of this country, for the benefit of the dairy industries, to keep
out oleomargarine. The producers of dairy foods recognized, during the war, that butter was very high, and serious objection was not raised then to the admission of oleomargarine. But it is well known that oleomargarine, on account of the way in which it is put up and its appearance, is often substituted and sold for butter. For that reason, the dairy interests of this country believe that the time has now arrived when they should oppose the admission of oleomargarine into Canada, and I will advise the Minister of Agriculture that when the Bill comes up for its second reading I will oppose it.

The hon. member for New Westminister (Mr. McQuarrie) was making a speech in favour of the protection of eggs in British Columbia. If he were here he would support me when I say that, when butter has gone down 20 cents a pound within a month or two, it is no time to allow the admission into this country of oleomargarine. For my part I wish to place myself on record as being opposed to the resolution.

In the past, a similar
resolution was before the House. I opposed it then, and to-day I am more opposed to this resolution, because the admission of oleomargarine into Canada will be hurtful to the dairy interests of our country. Until lately I did not know anything about oleomargarine, although I had heard a great deal about it. Lately I purchased some and tasted it. There is no flavour to it, and it is not a class of goods that should be used by anyone. On that account, and because of the inferiority of the goods I am opposed to the resolution.

This afternoon we
have had a great deal of discussion in regard to many articles of food and this and that, and now the Government is asking that oleomargarine may be sold in this country. As my hon. friend (Mr. Denis) has said, the price of butter has dropped 20 cents per pound or more within the last month or so, with the prospect of a still further drop in price. When butter is selling at such a low figure, it is not necessary to allow oleomargarine to be sold in this country. That was alright during the war when butter was high and the export of butter was at the highest point. As the matter stands now, we exported very little butter during 1920, and our exports this spring have been pretty low. Our wholesale houses are filled to the roof with butter, and it would be very unwise at this time

to allow again the importation and sale of oleomargarine. I wish to place myself on record as being opposed to the resolution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I suggest that we have an understanding that the passing of this resolution in no way commits the House to passing the Bill. We are simply advancing the matter a stage.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to, on division, and concurred in.
Mr. MEIGHEN thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 205, to amend the Oleomargarine Act, 1919, founded on the resolution.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext:
On motion of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen (Prime Minister), the House went into committee to consider the following resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to regulate the grading of Dairy Produce, and to provide,-
1.	That the Governor in Council may make regulations for the grading of dairy produce, that is to say, butter, cheese and other food products manufactured from milk intended for export; for the establishment or designation of grading stores; for the issuing of grader's certificates; for the special marking by manufacturers of packages of dairy produce intended to be graded; for the establishment of standards, definitions and grades for dairy prot duce; and, for the imposition of fees for the ' grading of dairy produce.
2.	That the Governor in Council may by regulation prescribe the time when any regulation made under the provisions of the proposed legislation shall come into operation, the particular kind or kinds of dairy produce to [DOT]which it shall apply, and the part or parts of Canada within which it shall be in force.
3.	That there may be appointed such dairy produce graders and other officers as may be deemed necessary for the carrying out of the provisions of the proposed legislation and of the regulations made thereunder.
4.	That the Governor in Council may by regulation provide for an appeal to the Dominion Dairy and Cold iStorage Commissioner, or his representative, from a decision of a Dairy Produce Grader as to the classification or grading of any particular lot of dairy produce.
5.	That penalties may be imposed for the violation of any provision of the proposed legislation or of any regulation made thereunder.

This resolution may be all right; but it is very wide and vague in its terms, and it should not be passed when, according to the rules, the committee is not supposed to sit. The committee is very slim, and there may be members who are not in the chamber at present, who would like to oppose the resolution.
[Mr. Dechene.J

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The resolution may be called "carried on division.'' There is this extra precaution in this case. The resolution has, of course, to be followed by a Bill, the same as the previous resolution; but this Bill would, I presume, have to go before the Committee on Agriculture, and there, as well as in the House, and in committee again, it will be threshed out, so that we are taking no risks.
1 Mr. ROBB: If as suggested by the Prime Minister, the resolution is passed on division, this time I would be compelled to vote with the Prime Minister. This matter has previously been before the Committee on Agriculture and it has been pretty well threshed out in that committee. While objection was taken to certain features of it, I think the Minister ol Agriculture and the Dairy Commissionei satisfied the Committee on Agriculture that nothing would be done that would be of any injury, and that this measure would be of advantage to the dairy industry As a representative of a dairying constituency, I am not opposed to the introduction of this measure, but I will reserve the right to determine my attitude when I see the Bill.

By passing this resolution, we commit ourselves, I suppose, to the principle of it. Is it the intention to make any new appointments or to impose any further burdens upon the country by reason of this legislation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If any new appointments are necessary, they will be in the nature of assistance to the country instead of burdens, but I must confess that I do not know.

That is the trouble of rushing through the business of the department. The minister (Mr. Tolmie) was here a few minutes ago, and he certainly is within call somewhere. He is not here now, although he should be here in order to give explanations.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to, on division.
Mr. Meighen thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 206, to regulate the grading of dairy produce, founded on the resolution.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
On t-he motion of Right Hon. Mr. Meighen the House adjourned at 6.18 p.m.

Monday, May 23, 1921.
